title: My entire indie game pipeline is basically AI now (Tripo + Codex + Claude + Blender)
author: ImportantAd4397
selftext:
I've been experimenting with an AI-first workflow for building our game over the past few weeks.

Surprisingly, it's becoming much more practical than I expected.

Here's roughly how the pipeline looks today:

**1. Character & Props**

* Tripo AI for rapid 3D asset generation
* Blender for cleanup, retopology and final adjustments

Instead of spending hours blocking out meshes, we can get a solid starting point within minutes.

**2. World Building**

We use a world model to brainstorm environments, level layouts and interactions before implementing anything.

It feels more like collaborating with a level designer than prompting an image model.

**3. Programming**

Codex handles:

* gameplay systems
* refactoring
* bug fixing
* repetitive implementation

Claude Sonnet is mostly my architecture reviewer.

Whenever I get stuck designing systems, Claude tends to produce cleaner abstractions.

  
**4. Polish**

Everything eventually goes through Blender.

Even AI-generated assets still need artist input.

The biggest productivity gain isn't replacing artists.

It's removing the blank canvas.



**What surprised me**

AI isn't replacing game developers.

It's replacing:

* searching StackOverflow
* writing boilerplate
* making placeholder assets
* repetitive iterations

The creative decisions are still ours.



Current stack:

* Tripo AI
* Codex
* Claude Sonnet
* Blender
* World Model

Curious what everyone else's workflow looks like.

comments.author: Tokiiz
comments.body: Is there any difference when it comes to the coding, using Claude vs Codex? I have always used Claude Code Sonnet/Opus when designing SaaS / Websites. Just started wth gamedev so not sure what LLM is best for this usecase.

replies.author: Sleazyweasel123
replies.body: ChatGPT is way better than Claude for game dev. (I use both) Easier to use (get your whole week upfront and it finishes tasks after you use all of your tokens), way way better at being creative, way better at drawing custom art.

replies.author: tuptain
replies.body: For me, Claude is my dev and Codex is my artist.

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body: Claude handles the big-picture design, system architecture, and lore/world logic really well, while Codex is great for drilling down into micro-implementations and specific gameplay scripts.

comments.author: paulordbm
comments.body: What world model do you use? Is it a local model you trained yourself? Could you elaborate a bit more? I use AI extensively in my web development work but am just starting using it for game dev and am really interested in hearing other people's experiences. I'm currently building my prototype with Claude, Blender and the Bevy Engine.

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body:
To clarify, it isn't a custom or locally trained model.

I mainly use Meshy for 3D environment generation, combined with Claude to plan out spatial layouts, level flow, and world logic before creating assets. In my setup, the 'world model' step is more about using these AI tools as a conceptual framework for level design, rather than running a self-hosted ML model.

That Claude, Blender, and Bevy stack sounds great though! How is Bevy working out for your prototyping?

comments.body:

comments.author: master_pk94
comments.body: Do you interact with AI prompting at every stage or is it like continuous integration pipeline?

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body:
Mostly prompting at every stage, except for the Blender/rendering step where it's traditional hands-on work.

For raw generation, design, world-building, and code, we prompt heavily to get 80% of the way there, then jump into Blender/IDE to polish. So it's very much a prompt-driven pipeline with manual artistic control.

comments.author: Acrobatic-Bit-1531
comments.body: not really the dev side of this but the "world model" question above is exactly what pulled me down this rabbit hole too, tbh. i do solo interactive stuff, not full games, and i bounce between a couple things depending on what i need. sillytavern still wins for straight up 1:1 character chat, nothing beats it there. worldos is the one i reach for when i want the whole setting to hold up, not just the one character i'm talking to, it actually keeps track of stuff i did two towns over instead of just resetting the second i change scenes. writing quality is a step down from a good character card though, i end up cleaning up half of what it gives me. still curious what an actual trained world model looks like under the hood, this thread has me wanting to know more

replies.author: Paran01d7Andr01d
replies.body: "World Model " same interest here. Ive been using Meshy to create characters and enemies, struggling with the world environment.  For context, also using Blender + Cursor

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body:
Meshy + Blender + Cursor is such a powerful combo.

The reason environments are so tricky compared to characters is that they require spatial continuity and structural logic, not just cool aesthetics. Using a world model at the start helps me nail down the scene's layout, interactive elements, and architectural breakdown so I know *exactly* what assets I need to generate/model next.

Are you struggling more with the spatial layout/design side, or the actual 3D environment asset pipeline?

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body: Spot on regarding the difference between isolated character chat and a persistent world state. That transition from single-card interactions to actual spatial and narrative memory is precisely why I lean on a world model for layout brainstorming. It’s definitely not a magic bullet out-of-the-box, but saving you from starting with a blank slate on macro-level design makes a massive difference. Appreciate you diving into this rabbit hole with us!

replies.author: ImportantAd4397
replies.body: Just AI tokens. I already have active subscriptions for those models.
